kernelIdea: f⁻¹ exists exactly when f is a bijection: surjectivity makes it total, injectivity makes it well-defined. The inverse of a bijection is a bijection.

kernels.l1: You can undo a machine only if nothing got mixed up and nothing got skipped.
kernels.l2: An undo-machine exists only when the first machine never shared and never skipped. Then every answer leads back to exactly one thing.
kernels.l3: A function can be undone exactly when it is a bijection. Being onto is what makes the undo-machine work on every answer, and being one-to-one is what makes each answer lead back to only one input.
kernels.l4: A function can be run backwards exactly when it is a perfect pairing. Being onto is what guarantees every element has something to go back to; being one-to-one is what makes that something unique. Running the reverse backwards returns the original.
kernels.l5: Invertibility is equivalent to bijectivity, and the two halves of the definition of function correspond exactly to the two halves of bijectivity.
kernels.l6: A function has a two-sided inverse under composition exactly when it is a bijection. Note that the symbol f⁻¹ is also used for pre-images, and those are a different object — a set rather than a value.
kernels.l7: A function is invertible exactly when it is bijective — surjectivity gives totality of the inverse, injectivity gives well-definedness. The inverse is itself a bijection with inverse f, and f⁻¹(t) as a value must not be confused with f⁻¹({t}) as a set.
kernels.l8: Invertibility is being an isomorphism in Set; f⁻¹ as inverse function and f⁻¹ as pre-image operator coincide notationally but not conceptually, the latter existing always.

kernel: f⁻¹ exists exactly when f is a bijection: surjectivity makes it total, injectivity makes it well-defined. The inverse of a bijection is a bijection, and its inverse is f again.
objectives: Explain why bijectivity is exactly the condition for invertibility
Prove the inverse of a bijection is a bijection
